headline: Egg Rock to the Graves: Bass Holding Deep, Bluefish Owning the Bunker
subhead: The harbor's bunker schools are pulling bluefish into a frenzy while the bass slide off into deeper water during the day — here's where and when to find both.
body_markdown:
If there's only one tide window this week, the call is the North Shore rocks over the harbor islands — Nahant, Egg Rock, and out to the Graves — fished on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, first light or last light. The harbor islands are still holding fish, but the daytime bite around Deer Island and Spectacle Island has gone quiet under a high sun, with bass sliding into the deeper holes off the flats and not committing again until the light drops. The North Shore's rocky structure holds shade and current all day, and that's where the bigger fish have been showing consistently.

We flagged this pattern last week and it's held — this is a summer holding pattern, not the fall run. Water temps are still comfortable, nights haven't cooled off enough to trigger the real push, and the striper population out there is spread thin but present, feeding on schedule around structure and current rather than blitzing open water. That changes once nighttime temps start dropping in earnest, likely mid-September, but for now the program is precision over volume.

Bluefish are the one species doing exactly what we said they'd do — tracking bunker density block for block. Pogy schools have been thick from President Roads down through the Winthrop side of the harbor and out past Deer Island Light, and the blues have been all over them, especially in the two hours around the top of the tide when the bait gets pushed up shallow. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters in the 2- to 3-ounce range — worked over visible bunker balls have been drawing fast, violent strikes, and chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig soaking bottom near the Deer Island flats has been picking off the bigger blues that hang under the schools rather than crashing the surface.

Striper-wise, the better fish are coming from the North Shore ledges on live mackerel and eels fished after dark. Egg Rock and the rock piles off Nahant have been giving up bass in the high 20s to low 30-inch range on live mackerel drifted or slow-trolled just off the structure in 15 to 25 feet, best on the last of the outgoing when current pulls bait off the rocks into deeper water. A few boats working the Graves and out toward Gloucester's outer ledges have connected on bigger fish — mid-30s and a few pushing 40 — on eels fished on a slow drift at night, working the tide change specifically, when the current slacks and the fish move up onto the rock to feed rather than holding tight against it.

Cape Ann's rocky shoreline from Bass Rocks down through Good Harbor and Brace Cove has been a mixed bag — some evenings the bass show hard on topwater plugs worked over the ledges at dusk, other nights it's dead calm with nothing showing until well after dark. That inconsistency tracks with what's happening region-wide: the fish are here, but they're not concentrated enough yet to fish predictably in daylight. Patience and putting in the dusk-to-dark window are paying off more than daytime effort right now.

Flounder have been steady but unspectacular on the harbor flats — Deer Island and the flats off Spectacle Island have produced fish in the 12- to 15-inch range on sandworms and clam bellies fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig, bottom bounced slow on the last of the ebb when the water's clean and the current isn't ripping. Nothing to build a trip around, but a solid option if the wind's up and the rocks are unfishable.

Looking at the next few days, expect more of the same pattern rather than a shift. The moon is building toward full, which should start pulling bait tighter and increasing tidal flow — worth watching closely because that's usually the trigger that gets bass to commit in bigger numbers rather than picking at bait individually. If that bait concentration happens the way it typically does heading into Labor Day week, look for the North Shore ledges and the harbor's bunker zones to both get more aggressive over the coming week. Wind out of the southwest has kept the water on the North Shore relatively clean; if that holds through the weekend, the dusk bite off Nahant and Egg Rock should stay productive.

For boat traffic heading into the holiday weekend, expect more pressure on the known spots — Deer Island Light, the Graves, and the bunker schools inside President Roads will get worked hard. If you want fish to yourself, the Cape Ann ledges north of Gloucester Harbor are seeing less pressure right now and still holding fish on the same eel-and-plug program after dark. Plymouth and Duxbury Bay remain a fallback for calmer water if wind kicks up out of the north, though nothing this week suggests they're outproducing the harbor or North Shore pattern currently in play.
